Heat-driven movement of dopant atoms through silicon along a concentration gradient.
Bombarding silicon with energetic dopant ions to set dose and depth.
Number of implanted ions per unit area, in ions/cm².
Short high-temperature anneal that activates dopants and repairs implant damage.
x<sub>ox</sub>² + A·x<sub>ox</sub> = B(t + τ): linear for thin oxide, parabolic for thick
x<sub>j</sub> = 2√(Dt)·√ln(C<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>B</sub>) for a Gaussian drive-in
Light-sensitive polymer exposed and developed to form a temporary mask pattern.
Patterned plate whose image is projected onto the wafer to expose resist.
Selective removal of a layer through openings in resist.
Etch that proceeds faster vertically than laterally, giving near-vertical sidewalls.
Adding a thin film such as oxide, nitride or metal to the wafer.
R = kλ/NA, DOF = λ/(2NA²)
Mask that defines the openings where gate oxide and transistors are formed.
Mask that patterns polysilicon gate electrodes and local interconnect.
All steps up to and including contact formation that build the transistors.
Metal interconnect and via steps after contacts that wire the transistors.
Y = e<sup>−A·D</sup> for die area A and defect density D
CMOS flow in which PMOS transistors sit in an n-well inside a p-substrate.
CMOS flow with separate n-well and p-well doping for independent NMOS and PMOS bodies.
γ = √(2qε<sub>Si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>)/C<sub>ox</sub>; heavier body doping gives a larger γ
Process that combines CMOS transistors with bipolar junction transistors on one die.
g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub>/V<sub>T</sub>, against 2I<sub>D</sub>/V<sub>ov</sub> for a MOSFET
Minimum width, spacing or overlap that keeps a layout shape manufacturable.
R = R<sub>s</sub>·L/W, sheet resistance times the number of squares
Dimensionless layer sketch where a poly crossing diffusion marks a transistor.
walk through every transistor edge once; its order is the poly column order
Parasitic p-n-p-n path that can short VDD to VSS in CMOS.
I × R<sub>sub</sub> or I × R<sub>well</sub> ≈ 0.7 V, and β<sub>npn</sub>·β<sub>pnp</sub> > 1

takeaways: Oxidation grows SiO₂, while diffusion and implantation introduce dopants; implantation sets dose and depth, diffusion drives dopants in, and the junction lies where the dopant meets the background doping.
Every patterned layer needs lithography, then either etch to remove material or deposition to add material.
A CMOS process flow is a fixed mask sequence; FEOL builds devices and BEOL wires them.
Well processes exist because NMOS and PMOS need opposite body doping.
BiCMOS adds a vertical NPN to the CMOS flow (buried layer and epitaxy first, base and emitter last) to get bipolar transconductance and drive beside CMOS logic.
Design rules expressed in λ keep drawn geometry inside lithography and etch limits.
A stick diagram shows topology only; each poly-diffusion crossing is a transistor.
Latch-up is a parasitic p-n-p-n thyristor; close taps, guard rings and spacing keep the well and substrate drops below 0.7 V so the loop never turns on.
bank_note: Long answers are marked for a correct mask-by-mask flow, the physical reason for each rule, and a clear latch-up prevention argument, not for memorised definitions alone.

bank.q: Explain thermal oxidation of silicon. Compare dry and wet oxidation and state where each is used in a CMOS flow.
outline: SiO₂ growth consumes silicon and forms a stable dielectric
Dry oxidation uses O₂, is slower and gives dense gate oxide
Wet oxidation uses H₂O vapour, is faster and gives thick field oxide
Deal-Grove model: linear for thin oxide, parabolic for thick
answer: Thermal oxidation heats silicon to 900–1100 °C in an oxidising gas. The oxidant diffuses through any oxide already present to the Si/SiO<sub>2</sub> interface and reacts there, so the new oxide forms at the bottom of the film and eats into the wafer: growing 1 μm of oxide uses about 0.44 μm of silicon, and the rest of the thickness rises above the old surface.

Two ambients are used. Dry oxidation: Si + O<sub>2</sub> → SiO<sub>2</sub>. Wet (steam) oxidation: Si + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>. Water molecules dissolve in oxide far more readily than oxygen, so wet growth is much faster.

answer.text: The Deal-Grove model gives the thickness x<sub>ox</sub> after time t:
answer.pre:
x<sub>ox</sub>² + A·x<sub>ox</sub> = B·(t + τ)
thin oxide:  x<sub>ox</sub> ≈ (B/A)·(t + τ)   linear, the surface reaction limits growth
thick oxide: x<sub>ox</sub> ≈ √(B·t)        parabolic, diffusion through the oxide limits growth

answer: A (μm) and B (μm²/h) depend on temperature and ambient; τ allows for oxide already present (and, in dry oxygen, for the fast initial growth). B/A is the linear rate constant and B the parabolic one.

answer.text: Comparison of the two ambients:

head: Property
Dry oxidation
Wet oxidation
rows: a few nm to tens of nm
gate oxide, pad and screen oxides

answer.text: Numbers at 1000 °C, ignoring τ (t = (x² + A·x)/B):

answer: Where each is used: the gate oxide is grown dry because a few nanometres of it set the threshold voltage and must have few traps and a controlled thickness; the slow rate is an advantage, since 9 minutes can be timed precisely. Field oxide must be thick to isolate neighbours, and only wet growth reaches 0.5 μm in about an hour; dry oxygen would need more than a day. Thin dry oxides also serve as the pad oxide under nitride and as a screen oxide during implants.

Silicon consumed: the 0.5 μm field oxide uses about 0.44 × 0.5 = 0.22 μm of silicon, so about 0.28 μm of it stands above the old surface; at the edge of a LOCOS window this step is the bird's beak and the height that later layers must cover.

Quality in practice: field oxides are often grown dry, then wet, then dry again, so the thick middle comes quickly while the faces next to the silicon and the top are dense. Gate oxides are grown dry, sometimes with a little chlorine to tie up sodium ions.
Check: wet growth of 0.5 μm takes 1.26 h against 28.4 h dry, about 22 times faster, which matches the rule that steam is used for thick films and oxygen for thin, high-quality ones.

bank.q: Describe the three unit processes that change the silicon: oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation. Give one CMOS step where each is used.
outline: Oxidation: grow SiO₂ for gate or field isolation
Diffusion: predeposition and drive-in; junction depth set by D·t and the background doping
Ion implantation: dose and energy set well, source and drain doping
Annealing activates dopants and repairs damage
answer: Oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation are the three steps that change the silicon itself. Lithography and etching only decide where they act. A CMOS flow uses all three, usually many times.

Oxidation grows SiO<sub>2</sub> by reacting the wafer with O<sub>2</sub> (dry, slow, dense) or steam (wet, fast) at 900–1100 °C. Growth follows the Deal-Grove model: linear in time while the film is thin, then parabolic. CMOS use: the dry gate oxide, a few nm thick; the wet field oxide that isolates devices; thin screen and pad oxides.

answer.text: Diffusion moves dopant atoms with heat. Fick's first law J = −D(∂C/∂x) gives the flux down the gradient; D = D<sub>0</sub>·exp(−E<sub>a</sub>/kT) rises steeply with temperature, roughly doubling every 30 °C near 1000 °C. It runs in two steps: predeposition with the surface at the solid solubility (an erfc profile), then drive-in from that fixed dose Q (a Gaussian):
Worked numbers (the drive-in of the chapter example: Q = 10¹⁴ cm⁻², D = 3×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s, 1 h, wafer N<sub>B</sub> = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³):

answer: CMOS use of diffusion: the well drive-in after the well implant, and every anneal that spreads dopants. Diffusion is isotropic, so the dopant also spreads sideways under the mask edge, nearly as far as it goes down.

answer.text: Ion implantation ionises dopant atoms, accelerates them to tens or hundreds of keV and fires them in. The dose φ (ions/cm²) is counted from the beam current, and the energy sets the projected range R<sub>p</sub> with straggle ΔR<sub>p</sub>:
Worked numbers (boron, φ = 10¹⁵ cm⁻², R<sub>p</sub> = 0.10 μm, ΔR<sub>p</sub> = 0.03 μm, into an n-well of 10¹⁷ cm⁻³):

answer: The wafer is tilted about 7° and rotated so ions do not channel between atom rows. Implanting damages the lattice, so a short anneal (seconds near 1000 °C) repairs it and activates the dopant. CMOS use: well implants, threshold-adjust implants, the lightly doped drain and the source/drain implants masked by the poly gate.

answer.text: Summary of where each step is used:

head: Process
What it does
Temperature
One CMOS step
rows: places a set dose at a set depth

answer: Temperature sensitivity: since D roughly doubles for every 30 °C near 1000 °C, running the same drive-in at 1030 °C gives D ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s and L = 0.208 × √2 = 0.294 μm. A furnace error of a few degrees therefore moves the junction measurably.

Predeposition sets the dose: with the surface held at the solid solubility C<sub>sol</sub>, the profile is C = C<sub>sol</sub>·erfc(x/2√(Dt)) and the dose that enters is Q = 2C<sub>sol</sub>√(Dt/π). The drive-in then spreads this fixed Q as the Gaussian above.

Anneal: after an implant the wafer is heated briefly (seconds near 1000 °C in a rapid thermal anneal). The heat repairs the lattice and activates the dopant, but it is itself a short diffusion, so its D·t must stay small compared with the depths wanted.
Check: the diffused junction (0.52 μm after one hour) is more than twice as deep as the implanted one (0.21 μm), which is why shallow source/drain junctions are implanted and wells are diffused.

bank.q: Explain the sequence lithography, then etch or deposition, for patterning one layer. Define photoresist, photomask, anisotropic etch and selectivity.
outline: Coat resist, expose through mask, develop pattern
Etch removes exposed layer; deposition adds a new film
Anisotropic etch gives vertical sidewalls
Selectivity means etch attacks the target layer faster than resist or underlayer
answer: One layer is patterned by the same loop every time: lithography prints the pattern in resist, then the layer below is etched or a new layer is deposited, and the resist is stripped.

Photoresist is a light-sensitive polymer spun onto the wafer, usually under 1 μm thick. In a positive resist the exposed part dissolves in the developer; in a negative resist the exposed part cross-links and stays.
A photomask is a glass plate carrying the pattern of one layer in chrome. A 1× mask is the wafer size; a reticle carries a 4× or 5× pattern that the projection lens reduces.
The lithography steps: clean and dehydrate the wafer; spin-coat resist; soft bake; align the mask to the previous layer; expose with UV light; develop; then etch or deposit, and strip the resist.

answer.text: Resolution and depth of focus set the smallest feature: R = k·λ/NA and DOF = λ/(2NA²). For the chapter example (λ = 248 nm, k = 0.6):

answer: A larger NA prints finer lines but focuses over a shallower range, so the wafer must be flat; this is why CMP planarises the surface before critical layers.

Etching removes the layer through the resist window. Wet etching is isotropic and undercuts the resist. Dry etching (RIE) combines a reactive plasma with ion bombardment of the floor, so it is anisotropic. Anisotropy is A = 1 − (lateral rate/vertical rate): A = 1 is a vertical wall, A = 0 an isotropic etch.

Selectivity is the etch rate of the target layer divided by the etch rate of the mask or the layer below. A high selectivity lets the etch finish, and over-etch, without eating through the resist or the underlayer.

answer.text: Worked numbers (0.5 μm oxide, 2.0 μm window, 100 nm/min, selectivity 5 : 1, 20 % over-etch):

answer: Deposition adds a film instead: LPCVD for conformal poly and nitride at high temperature, PECVD for oxide and nitride at low temperature over metal, sputtering for aluminium and barrier metals, and epitaxy for single-crystal silicon.
Positive resist is the usual choice for fine features because the developer does not swell it; negative resist was used in older processes and for some thick patterns.
Flatness: with the NA = 0.6 lens the DOF is 344 nm, so the step left by a 0.5 μm field oxide is already larger than the depth of focus; CMP polishes the steps away before critical layers are printed.
Check: the wet hole grows by 1.2 μm, sixty per cent of the window, so fine lines must be cut by RIE; 120 nm of resist lost is well under a typical 1 μm coat, so the 5 : 1 selectivity is enough.

bank.q: Define a design rule and λ. State four typical layout rules for diffusion, poly, contact and metal.
outline: Design rule is a minimum width, spacing or overlap
λ is the scalable layout unit
Rules cover diffusion width, poly spacing, contact enclosure and metal spacing
Rules prevent shorts, opens and unreliable contacts
answer: A design rule is a minimum width, spacing, overlap, enclosure or extension that a drawn shape must obey so that its mask prints, aligns and etches without breaks or shorts. The rule set is a contract between the designer and the foundry: a layout that obeys it can be made.

Rules exist because printing is imperfect. Masks land slightly off the layer below (misalignment), etching moves edges in or out (etch bias), and the printer cannot form features below some size (finite resolution). A rule is a margin against these errors.

λ (lambda) is a single length unit chosen for the process, usually half the smallest drawn feature (half the minimum channel length). Every rule is a whole multiple of λ, so a layout drawn in λ moves to a new process by changing one number: these are scalable design rules. Production processes publish micron rules in absolute units instead, which are tighter and layer-specific.
λ is not the wavelength of the lithography light; in a layout question it is only the drawing unit.

answer.text: Typical λ rules (exact values differ a little between rule sets):

head: Layer
Rule
Value
Reason
rows: line must not break; neighbours must not short
misalignment must not short source to drain
spacing when not forming a gate
size; enclosure by metal, poly or active
contact must land fully on both layers
wider for the rougher metal etch

answer.text: Converting to micrometres with λ = 0.5 μm (the chapter example):

answer: The rules are checked by a design rule checker (DRC), which tests every shape on every layer against the rule deck before the layout is sent to the fab.

Reading a rule set: each rule names a layer or a pair of layers, a type (width, spacing, enclosure, extension, overlap) and a value. A drawn metal line 2λ wide against a 3λ rule is a width violation; two poly lines 1λ apart against a 2λ rule are a spacing violation.

Why metal rules are larger than poly rules: metal is thicker and its etch is rougher, and the metal lies over a less flat surface, so its edges move more. Poly sets the channel length, so it is held to the tightest rule the lithography allows.
Check: with C<sub>ox</sub> = 2.3 fF/μm² the minimum transistor above has a gate capacitance of 2.3 × 4 = 9.2 fF, so the rules fix not only area but also the load each gate presents.

bank.q: Draw a stick diagram for a CMOS inverter and a two-input NAND gate. Mark active, poly, metal and contact layers.
outline: One line per layer, no dimensions
Poly crossing diffusion marks a transistor
PMOS in n-well, NMOS in p-substrate or p-well
VDD and VSS rails, input and output connections
NAND has series NMOS and parallel PMOS
answer: A stick diagram shows each layer as a line with no dimensions: diffusion green, poly red (orange in the figure below), metal blue, and a contact as a dot. A poly line crossing diffusion is a transistor. VDD runs along the top in metal and VSS along the bottom; the pMOS strip sits near VDD (inside the n-well) and the nMOS strip near VSS.

Inverter, y = ¬a. The pull-down is one nMOS from y to VSS; the pull-up is one pMOS from y to VDD. Stick: one poly column a crosses both strips. The p-strip runs VDD | a | y and the n-strip VSS | a | y. Contacts drop from the VDD rail to the p-strip source and from the VSS rail to the n-strip source; a metal line joins the two y contacts and is the output.
NAND, y = ¬(a·b). The output is 0 only when a = b = 1, so the nMOS are in series (y–a–n1–b–VSS). The pMOS are the dual: in parallel from y to VDD.

Column order by the Euler path: the n-graph has edges a: y–n1 and b: n1–VSS, odd vertices y and VSS, path y–a–n1–b–VSS. The p-graph has edges a: y–VDD and b: VDD–y, every degree even, closed trail y–a–VDD–b–y. Both use the order a, b, so two poly columns serve both strips with no break.

svg.aria: Two stick diagrams. Inverter: one poly column a across a p strip from VDD to y and an n strip from VSS to y, with the two y contacts joined in metal. NAND: poly columns a and b; the p strip runs y, a, VDD, b, y and the n strip runs y, a, n1, b, VSS, with metal joining the y contacts.

answer.text: What each NAND contact does:

head: Strip
Node
Contact?
Connection
rows: metal back to the left y
shared diffusion between the two nMOS

answer: Count check: the inverter has 1 + 1 = 2 transistors, so 2 poly-diffusion crossings; the NAND has 2 + 2 = 4, so 4 crossings, two per poly column.

How to draw any stick diagram: (1) write the pull-down network from the function and the pull-up as its dual; (2) draw each as a graph and find a common Euler path; (3) draw the VDD rail, the p-strip, the n-strip and the VSS rail; (4) draw one poly column per input in the path order, crossing both strips; (5) add contacts to the rails and to the output nodes; (6) join the output contacts in metal and mark the n-well round the p-strip.
Inverter layout width, with the same rules: p-strip 1 + 2 (contact) + 2 + 2 (gate) + 2 + 2 (contact) + 1 = 12λ, that is 6 μm for λ = 0.5 μm.

Common mistakes: drawing the NAND pMOS in series (that is the NOR); forgetting the metal link between the two y ends of the p-strip, which leaves one pMOS drain floating; putting a contact on n1, which is harmless but costs area; and letting a poly column end before it crosses both strips, which leaves out a transistor.

From stick to layout: with contact 2λ, 1λ of diffusion beyond a contact, 2λ from contact to gate, 2λ poly and 3λ between gates that share an uncontacted node, the NAND p-strip is 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 20λ long and the n-strip 17λ, so the cell is about 20λ = 10 μm wide for λ = 0.5 μm.

bank.q: Given the mask sequence active, poly, n-select, p-select, contact, metal, describe the layer added or doping made by each mask in an n-well CMOS flow.
outline: Active defines transistor openings
Poly forms gates and local interconnect
n-select blocks or opens NMOS source and drain doping
p-select opens PMOS source and drain doping
Contact opens windows to silicon or poly; metal wires them
answer: In an n-well flow on a p-type wafer, the n-well mask comes first, before the masks in the list: it opens the PMOS areas for a phosphorus implant and a long drive-in. The listed masks then follow in order; each is one lithography step that opens resist (or leaves it) where one process acts.

answer.text: What each mask does:

head: Mask
Process it guides
What it makes
rows: nitride kept on the active islands; field oxide grown (LOCOS) or trenches cut and filled (STI) elsewhere
the islands where transistors sit, isolated by thick oxide
after gate oxide and poly deposition, the poly is etched
resist opened over the NMOS areas for an arsenic or phosphorus implant
n<sup>+</sup> source and drain, n<sup>+</sup> well taps
resist opened over the PMOS areas for a boron implant
p<sup>+</sup> source and drain, p<sup>+</sup> substrate taps
holes etched in the oxide over the wafer
openings from metal down to diffusion and poly

answer: Self-alignment: the select masks only decide which transistor gets which implant. The source/drain edges are set by the poly gate (with its spacers), which blocks the implant under itself, so the select masks can be drawn loosely, a few λ beyond the active.

The two select masks must be separate. If one implant reached the other transistor, n<sup>+</sup> donors in a p<sup>+</sup> region (or the reverse) would compensate the doping and raise the source/drain resistance, or even change its type.

The taps come from the same masks: an n<sup>+</sup> tap in the n-well (n-select) ties the well to VDD, and a p<sup>+</sup> tap in the substrate (p-select) ties it to VSS. No extra mask is needed for them.

After the implants, an anneal activates the dopants. Only then are contacts opened, because metal cannot take the anneal temperature. Contacts are etched where metal must reach silicon or poly, and the metal mask then patterns the wiring.
The full order is therefore: n-well, active, poly, n-select, p-select, contact, metal (plus via, metal 2 and pad masks in a two-metal process, ten in all).

Alignment: the active mask carries the first alignment marks; poly is aligned to active, the two select masks and the contact mask to poly and active, and metal to contact. Only the poly-to-active alignment is critical, because the source/drain edges come from the gate itself.

Cross-section after each step, in words: after active, islands of bare silicon are surrounded by thick oxide; after poly, a thin gate line crosses each island; after the select implants, the island on each side of every gate is n<sup>+</sup> or p<sup>+</sup>; after contact, holes reach those regions through the oxide on top; after metal, aluminium fills the holes and runs between them.
Lightly doped drains: in most flows an LDD implant and an oxide spacer come between poly and the select implants. They use the same select masks, so the list of masks does not change.

Check: seven masks make a one-metal CMOS inverter; each transistor needs active and poly, the two select masks split the implants, and contact and metal wire it up, so no mask in the list can be dropped.

bank.q: Compare n-well, p-well and twin-tub CMOS processes. For each, state substrate type, well type and one advantage or limitation.
outline: n-well: p-substrate, PMOS in n-well, NMOS native substrate
p-well: n-substrate, NMOS in p-well, PMOS native substrate
Twin-tub: both wells, independent body doping
Twin-tub costs more masks but balances transistor performance
answer: An NMOS needs a p-type body and a PMOS an n-type body. One wafer has one doping, so at least one device must sit in a locally doped well. The three processes differ in which device gets the well.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: n-well
p-well
twin-tub
rows: n-well and p-well, each doped separately
NMOS keeps high mobility and a small body effect; grew from nMOS processes
PMOS in the substrate; a well that isolates the NMOS
both thresholds and body effects set independently
PMOS pays for the well doping
NMOS has the higher body effect and lower mobility
one more mask and a longer thermal budget

answer.text: The body doping matters. With t<sub>ox</sub> = 10 nm (C<sub>ox</sub> = 3.45×10⁻⁷ F/cm²) and γ = √(2qε<sub>Si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>)/C<sub>ox</sub>:

answer: So a twin-tub process can choose each well dose to set the threshold and the body effect of its own device, where an n-well process takes whatever the substrate gives the NMOS.
Taps: the n-well (or n-substrate) goes to VDD through n<sup>+</sup> taps and the p-substrate (or p-well) to VSS through p<sup>+</sup> taps, so every well-substrate junction stays reverse biased.

Latch-up: all three contain the parasitic p-n-p-n path; the well and substrate resistances decide how easily it fires, so tap spacing is a rule in every one of them. A p-epi layer on a p<sup>+</sup> wafer, common in n-well and twin-tub processes, lowers the substrate resistance.
Choice: n-well dominates digital CMOS; twin-tub is used where both devices need tuning (low-voltage, analog and mixed-signal); p-well is now rare.

Junction capacitance: for a one-sided n<sup>+</sup>-p junction the depletion width varies as 1/√N<sub>A</sub>, so the capacitance per area varies as √N<sub>A</sub>. The NMOS drain in a 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ p-well has about √100 = 10 times the capacitance per area of one in the 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ substrate, which slows the gate it drives.

Area: a twin-tub layout must space the two wells and keep each transistor well inside its own well, so a CMOS cell is a little larger; an n-well layout needs spacing only between the n-well edge and the NMOS diffusions.

Cross-section, n-well inverter: a p-substrate with an n-well; in the well a PMOS with p<sup>+</sup> source and drain and an n<sup>+</sup> tap to VDD; outside it an NMOS with n<sup>+</sup> source and drain and a p<sup>+</sup> tap to VSS; one poly line forms both gates and the two drains are joined in metal as the output. The twin-tub version adds a p-well round the NMOS and its tap.
Check: the heavier p-well gives √100 = 10 times the γ, and with its larger 2φ<sub>F</sub> about nine times the threshold shift (0.23 V against 0.026 V), consistent with γ ∝ √N<sub>A</sub>.

bank.q: A layout violates a poly-to-active spacing rule. Explain how design rule checking catches it and why the spacing matters physically.
outline: DRC compares drawn edges against a rule table
Poly-to-active spacing protects gate oxide and source-drain regions
Too-small spacing risks lithography bridging or etch damage
Fix by moving or resizing the poly or active shape
answer: The rule: a poly line that does not form a gate must keep a minimum spacing from the active (diffusion) area, typically 1λ. With λ = 0.5 μm that is 0.5 μm.

How DRC catches it: the design rule checker reads the layout file and rebuilds each layer as polygons. For this rule it takes every poly edge that does not cross active and measures the distance to the nearest active edge. Any gap below 1λ is reported as a violation, with the rule name and the coordinates of the two shapes, and a marker is drawn on the layout. The design cannot be signed off until every marker is cleared.

Why the spacing matters physically: the poly mask and the active mask are separate masks, so they can be misaligned against each other by about a λ. If a poly line drawn 0.25 μm from the active shifts by 0.3 μm, it lands on the active and crosses diffusion. A poly-diffusion crossing is always a transistor, so an unwanted transistor appears, or the poly edge blocks part of a source/drain implant and narrows the diffusion.

Etch bias adds to the risk: if each edge prints up to 0.1 μm wider than drawn, the gap loses another 0.1 μm or more. At the edge of a LOCOS field oxide the bird's beak also makes the active boundary uncertain.

answer.text: The numbers for a drawn gap of 0.5λ:

answer: Fix: move the poly line, or narrow it where it runs beside the active, until the gap is at least 1λ; if the poly must pass, route it in metal instead. Then run DRC again until the deck reports no errors.

Related rules on the same pair of layers: poly must extend about 2λ past the active where it forms a gate, so a misaligned gate still cuts the channel completely; active must extend about 3λ past the gate for the source and drain contacts; and poly must keep a spacing from a contact to active so the gate never touches the contact.
Check: with the drawn 1λ = 0.5 μm gap, the same 0.1 μm bias and 0.3 μm misalignment leave 0.1 μm, still positive, which is what the rule is sized for.

bank.q: Explain how a vertical NPN is added to a CMOS flow in BiCMOS. State two circuit benefits and one process cost.
outline: Add buried layer and epitaxy before the wells, a sinker, then base and emitter after the CMOS steps
NPN gives high current drive; CMOS gives high input impedance
Extra masks and thermal steps raise cost
BiCMOS suits analog-digital and high-drive interfaces
answer: BiCMOS puts a vertical NPN beside the CMOS devices on one die. The CMOS part is unchanged; the NPN needs a lightly doped collector and a way to take collector current out with little resistance.

answer.text: The process steps, in order:

head: Step
Mask
What it makes
rows: n<sup>+</sup> arsenic or antimony implant in the p-substrate, under the future NPN
n-type epitaxial layer grown over it: the lightly doped collector
deep n<sup>+</sup> implant, driven down to the buried layer by the well drive-in
n-well and p-well for the CMOS devices
the CMOS transistors, then the source/drain anneal
shallow p implant for the NPN base
shallow n<sup>+</sup> implant inside the base
wiring for both kinds of device

answer: Order: the buried layer must face the hot epitaxy and well drive-in, so it comes first; the base is a few tenths of a micrometre deep and would spread in those hot steps, so it comes after them. Electrons flow from the emitter down through the thin base, along the buried layer and up the sinker to the collector contact.

answer.text: Benefit 1, transconductance. At the same current, g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub>/V<sub>T</sub> for the NPN against g<sub>m</sub> = 2I<sub>D</sub>/V<sub>ov</sub> for a MOSFET:

answer: Benefit 2, drive and precision. Large g<sub>m</sub> lets a bipolar stage drive heavy loads and long lines quickly, and V<sub>BE</sub> stays close to 0.7 V over a wide current range, which gives good references, current mirrors and comparators. CMOS keeps its zero DC input current, dense logic and low static power on the same die.

Process cost: three or four extra masks (buried layer, sinker, base, emitter), an epitaxy step, and a tighter thermal budget, since every step after the base must stay short and cool. More steps mean longer cycle time, higher wafer cost and lower yield.
BiCMOS therefore suits radio front ends, high-speed drivers and links, mixed-signal chips and power ICs with bipolar references.

Isolation: each NPN sits in its own n-epi island, surrounded by p-type regions tied to VSS, so neighbours are separated by reverse-biased junctions. In a BiCMOS flow the wells and channel-stop implants can provide this, but the isolation still adds area round every bipolar device.

Base width and β: β rises as the base gets thinner and more lightly doped, because fewer electrons recombine on the way across. A thin base also shortens the transit time, so the NPN is faster; but too thin a base punches through at a low collector voltage. The late, shallow base implant is what lets the process set this width.

Why the epi is lightly doped: the base-collector junction must hold the supply with margin, and light collector doping widens its depletion region into the epi. The epi thickness is then chosen so this depletion region does not reach the buried layer at the working voltage.
Check: the ratio 76.9/8 = 9.6 equals 0.5 V/(2 × 26 mV) = 9.6, so the advantage does not depend on the current chosen.

bank.q: Analyze latch-up in a CMOS inverter using the parasitic p-n-p-n structure. Explain the role of Rwell and Rsubstrate and give four layout prevention methods.
outline: parasitic p-n-p and n-p-n form a thyristor
Rwell and Rsubstrate sustain the regenerative loop
Guard rings collect injected carriers
Body taps reduce well and substrate resistance
Wider spacing and majority-carrier guards raise holding current

answer.text: Structure. In an n-well CMOS inverter the p<sup>+</sup> PMOS source (at VDD), the n-well, the p-substrate and the n<sup>+</sup> NMOS source (at VSS) form a p-n-p-n stack. Inside it sit two parasitic bipolar transistors:

answer: Each collector feeds the other's base: the npn collector is the n-well (the pnp base), and the pnp collector is the substrate (the npn base). The pair is a thyristor (SCR) between VDD and VSS.

Role of R<sub>well</sub> and R<sub>sub</sub>. R<sub>well</sub> is the well resistance from the pnp base region to the nearest n<sup>+</sup> well tap; R<sub>sub</sub> is the substrate resistance from the npn base region to the nearest p<sup>+</sup> tap. A current through R<sub>sub</sub> raises the local substrate above VSS by I × R<sub>sub</sub>; a current through R<sub>well</sub> pulls the local well below VDD by I × R<sub>well</sub>. When either drop reaches about 0.7 V, that transistor's emitter-base junction turns on.
Trigger. A current spike from a pad, an input undershoot below VSS or overshoot above VDD, a fast supply ramp, or radiation injects carriers into the substrate or well.

answer.text: Numbers (I<sub>inj</sub> = 2 mA, β<sub>npn</sub> = 50, β<sub>pnp</sub> = 20):

head: Case
Working
Result
rows: below 0.7 V: npn off, no latch-up

answer: Regeneration. Once the npn conducts, its collector current flows through R<sub>well</sub> and turns the pnp on; the pnp collector current flows through R<sub>sub</sub> and holds the npn on. With β<sub>npn</sub> × β<sub>pnp</sub> > 1 each pass round the loop adds current, until only the supply limits it. The path stays on after the trigger ends (if the current exceeds the holding current), and only removing power resets it. The chip may reset, or the large current may melt metal.

Layout prevention 1, taps close to every device: p<sup>+</sup> substrate taps tied to VSS near each NMOS and n<sup>+</sup> well taps tied to VDD near each PMOS. What counts is the distance from the injection point to the nearest tap. Example: a 20 μm wide well of 1 kΩ per square, 0.2 mA injected and a 0.3 V limit allow 1500 Ω, which is 1.5 squares, so a tap within 30 μm.

Layout prevention 2, guard rings: a p<sup>+</sup> ring tied to VSS round the NMOS and an n<sup>+</sup> ring tied to VDD round the PMOS collect the injected carriers before they reach a parasitic base, and lower the local resistance.

Layout prevention 3, spacing: keeping NMOS n<sup>+</sup> diffusions farther from the n-well edge widens the base of the lateral npn and lowers its β, so I/O cells, which see the outside world, use much larger n-well to n<sup>+</sup> spacings.
Layout prevention 4, place I/O and drivers away from the core logic, with their own guard rings and supply pads, so injected current is collected at the edge of the die.

Process help: a thin p-epi layer on a p<sup>+</sup> substrate makes R<sub>sub</sub> small; a retrograde well puts heavy doping at the well bottom, lowering R<sub>well</sub> and β<sub>pnp</sub>; trench isolation lengthens the lateral path; SOI removes the path altogether.

Holding condition: once latched, the SCR stays on as long as the supply can provide more than the holding current through a voltage above the holding voltage. If the holding voltage is above the supply, the path cannot stay latched, which is one way I/O cells are made safe.

Current-injection test: current is forced into (and out of) each pin in turn, for example ±100 mA, with the supply at its maximum. The injection is then removed and the supply current is measured; if it stays high, the chip has latched. The test is run hot, since β rises and the junction turn-on voltage falls with temperature.

Where it bites: I/O pads, which see undershoot, overshoot and electrostatic events, and any place where large drivers sit next to logic. A layout puts guard rings round every I/O transistor and keeps the core well away from the pad ring.
Check: halving R<sub>sub</sub> from 500 Ω to 250 Ω gives 2 mA × 250 Ω = 0.5 V, below 0.7 V, so taps placed twice as close turn the latching case into a safe one.

bank.q: Evaluate why a process flow fixes mask order by temperature and alignment. Give examples of steps that must come before others.
outline: High-temperature steps come before low-temperature metal
Each mask aligns to an earlier reference layer
Gate oxide must form after well drive-in
Contacts open after transistor and dielectric formation
Metal must come after contacts and vias
answer: The order of a CMOS flow is fixed by two things: temperature (each step must survive every later step) and alignment (each mask must line up with a pattern that already exists).

Thermal budget: dopant profiles keep moving at every hot step, and metal cannot take high temperatures (aluminium melts at 660 °C and reacts with silicon well below that). So the hottest, longest steps go first and the coolest last.

answer.text: Typical steps in order, with their temperatures:

head: Step
Typical temperature
Why it sits here
rows: deepest diffusion; must not disturb anything made later
isolation must exist before devices are placed
after the long hot steps, so it stays thin and clean
needs the gate oxide under it
room temperature, then about 1000 °C for seconds
need the poly gate as the mask
metal comes after every high-temperature step

answer: Examples of "must come before": the well before the gate oxide (the well drive-in would thicken and contaminate an oxide already grown); the gate oxide before poly (poly is deposited on it); poly before the source/drain implant (the gate is the implant mask, which makes source and drain self-aligned); the activation anneal before contacts (metal cannot take it); contacts before metal 1, and vias before metal 2 (metal fills the holes).

Alignment: the first mask (well or active) sets alignment marks; every later mask is aligned to a layer already on the wafer, usually active or poly, within a tolerance of about one λ. A layer cannot be aligned to one that does not exist yet, so the layers that others land on (active, poly) come early.

Self-alignment removes one alignment from the critical path: because the poly gate blocks the source/drain implant, the source and drain edges are fixed by the gate itself, not by a separate mask, and the n-select and p-select masks can be drawn with loose margins.
BiCMOS shows the same logic: the buried layer goes before the epitaxy and well drive-in because it must be driven deep, and the shallow base goes after them so it does not spread.

Evaluation: a different order would either destroy a finished structure (a shallow junction spread by a later drive-in, aluminium melted by an anneal) or leave a mask with nothing to align to. Process engineers can shorten steps, for example by using rapid thermal anneals, but they cannot swap them.

Isolation order: in a LOCOS flow the field oxide is grown before the gate oxide because it is the longest oxidation; in an STI flow the trench is etched, filled and polished before the wells or right after them, because CMP needs a flat surface with no devices on it.

Spacer and LDD order: the light LDD implant uses the bare gate as its mask; the oxide spacer is then formed and the heavy source/drain implant uses gate plus spacer. Swapping them would put the heavy implant right at the gate edge and lose the low-field drain.

Silicide: where it is used, titanium, cobalt or nickel is reacted with the exposed silicon and poly after the source/drain anneal and before the first dielectric, at a few hundred degrees; earlier would be too hot for it, later the silicon would be covered.
Back-end alignment: each metal layer is aligned to the contacts or vias below it, and each via layer to the metal below, so the back end is a chain in which every mask lands on the one just made.
Check: the ten masks of a two-metal flow (n-well, active, poly, n<sup>+</sup>, p<sup>+</sup>, contact, metal 1, via, metal 2, pad) run from the hottest steps to the coolest, in exactly this logic.

bank.q: Compare ion implantation with thermal diffusion for source and drain doping. Discuss dose control, lateral spread, damage and annealing.
outline: Implantation gives precise dose and energy
Diffusion gives deeper, more lateral spread
Implant damages crystal lattice and needs anneal
Diffusion needs high thermal budget
Advanced CMOS relies on implantation plus rapid anneal
answer: Source and drain must be shallow, heavily doped and placed exactly at the gate edge. Both thermal diffusion and ion implantation can dope them; modern CMOS uses implantation, and the comparison shows why.

answer.text: Dose control. Implantation counts the ions directly: the dose is the integrated beam current divided by the charge per ion and the wafer area, set to about one per cent anywhere from 10¹¹ to 10¹⁶ cm⁻². Diffusion from a gas source fixes the surface at the solid solubility, so the dose depends on temperature and time and is hard to set at low values.
answer.pre:
implant: φ = (I × t)/(q × area)
diffusion: Q set by solubility, temperature and time

answer: Depth control. The implant depth is set by the energy through R<sub>p</sub> and ΔR<sub>p</sub>; diffusion depth is set by D·t, and D changes by a factor of two for every 30 °C near 1000 °C.

Lateral spread. Diffusion is isotropic: the dopant moves sideways under the mask edge nearly as far as it goes down (about 0.8 x<sub>j</sub>), which would push source and drain under the gate and shorten the channel. Implantation is directional: the lateral straggle is of the order of ΔR<sub>p</sub>, and the only extra spread comes from the anneal.

answer.text: Numbers from the chapter examples:

head: Diffusion (1 h, 1000 °C)
Implantation (boron)
rows: thick oxide (resist cannot take the heat)
resist, oxide or the poly gate (0.22 μm of oxide is enough)

answer: Damage and annealing. Implanted ions knock silicon atoms off their sites and can leave an amorphous layer; until annealed, many dopants are not on lattice sites and do not conduct. An anneal (rapid thermal, seconds near 1000 °C) repairs the lattice and activates the dopant. Diffusion causes no such damage, since the atoms arrive by heat.

Thermal budget. Diffusion needs long hot steps that move every earlier profile; implantation is done at room temperature and needs only the short anneal, which keeps the wells and threshold implants where they were placed.

Masking and alignment. A resist mask can block an implant, so the n<sup>+</sup> and p<sup>+</sup> implants are separated by the select masks, and the poly gate itself blocks the implant under it: the source and drain are self-aligned to the gate. Channelling is avoided by tilting the wafer about 7°.

Lightly doped drain: a modern source/drain is made in two implants. A light n<sup>−</sup> implant uses the bare poly gate as its mask; an oxide spacer is formed; then the heavy n<sup>+</sup> implant uses gate plus spacer. The light region under the spacer lowers the peak electric field at the drain and the hot-carrier damage it causes. Only implantation can make this pair, because each dose and depth must be set separately.

Comparison at a glance: diffusion gives a deep, graded junction with a large sideways spread and no damage; implantation gives a set dose, a shallow junction and a sharp edge, at the cost of damage that must be annealed.

Conclusion: implantation gives a set dose, a shallow junction and little sideways spread with a small thermal budget, so it is used for source/drain, LDD, threshold-adjust and well implants; diffusion survives as the drive-in and anneal that follow. Check: the implanted junction (0.214 μm) is less than half the diffused one (0.522 μm) despite ten times the dose.

bank.q: A twin-tub CMOS process is changed to an n-well process. Analyze which transistor body doping and well spacing rules change, and one effect on latch-up.
outline: NMOS body becomes p-substrate instead of p-well
PMOS still sits in n-well
Well-to-well spacing rules simplify or disappear
Substrate tap and well tap placement affect parasitic resistance
Latch-up immunity may change with body doping and spacing
answer: In the twin-tub process the NMOS sits in a p-well and the PMOS in an n-well, each doped separately. Changing to an n-well process removes the p-well: the NMOS is built directly in the lightly doped p-substrate, and the PMOS stays in the n-well.

answer.text: NMOS body doping falls from the p-well value to the substrate value. With C<sub>ox</sub> = 3.45×10⁻⁷ F/cm²:

answer: Effects on the NMOS: the body effect falls about nine-fold; the threshold voltage falls too, so a threshold-adjust implant (boron) is usually added to set it; the source/drain junction capacitance falls because the depletion region in the lighter body is wider; the electron mobility rises slightly with less impurity scattering.
PMOS: unchanged; it stays in the n-well, with the same well doping, taps and threshold.
Masks: one fewer well mask, and a shorter thermal budget without the p-well drive-in.

Design rules that change: the rules that involve the p-well disappear (p-well width and spacing, p-well enclosure of n<sup>+</sup> active, and the p-well to n-well spacing or overlap at the well boundary). The n-well rules stay: n-well minimum width, n-well enclosure of p<sup>+</sup> active, and n-well to n<sup>+</sup> active spacing, which also sets how close an NMOS may sit to the well.

answer.text: Effect on latch-up: the npn base is now the lightly doped substrate, whose resistance is higher than that of a p-well, and the npn β can rise. For the same 2 mA injection:

answer: So a substrate that is 2.5 times more resistive turns a safe layout into one that can latch. The n-well process must therefore keep R<sub>sub</sub> small: closer p<sup>+</sup> substrate taps, guard rings round the NMOS, or a p-epi wafer on a heavily doped p<sup>+</sup> substrate.

Threshold: φ<sub>F</sub> falls from 0.417 V to 0.298 V and the depletion charge under the gate falls ten-fold, so the NMOS threshold drops by a few tenths of a volt. A boron threshold-adjust implant, masked to the NMOS areas, restores it; this mask is often already in the flow.

Junction capacitance: for an n<sup>+</sup>-p junction the capacitance per area varies as √N<sub>A</sub>, so moving the NMOS from a 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ p-well to a 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ substrate cuts its drain capacitance per area by about √100 = 10. The gates it drives switch faster.
Body bias: in the twin-tub process the p-well could, in a triple-well variant, be biased on its own; in the n-well process every NMOS shares the one substrate, so its body is always at VSS.
Layout area: without the p-well boundary, the NMOS can sit closer to the n-well edge (only the n-well to n<sup>+</sup> spacing remains), so a standard cell may become slightly shorter.

Conclusion: the change saves a mask and gives a faster NMOS with less body effect, at the cost of losing independent control of the NMOS threshold and of needing more care with substrate taps for latch-up. Check: γ scales as √N<sub>A</sub>, so a 100-fold drop in doping gives a ten-fold drop in γ (0.53 to 0.053 V<sup>½</sup>).

bank.q: Evaluate stick diagrams as a first layout step. What information they preserve and what they omit, and how design rules enter later.
outline: Preserve layer topology, transistor order and connections
Omit dimensions, exact widths and spacing
Help compare alternative gate layouts quickly
Design rules fix final widths, spacings and overlaps
Stick diagram becomes a mask layout after rule-driven sizing
answer: A stick diagram is the first layout step: it shows each layer of a cell as a line (diffusion, poly, metal), contacts as dots, the VDD and VSS rails, and nothing else.

What it preserves: the topology. It shows which transistors exist (every poly-diffusion crossing), which diffusion segments two transistors share, the order of the poly columns along each strip, where contacts go and how nodes are wired in metal. These decide the electrical behaviour, the number of contacts and the number of diffusion breaks.

What it omits: every dimension. Widths, lengths, spacings and enclosures are not shown, nor transistor sizing (W/L), nor the exact positions of wires. A stick diagram cannot be checked by DRC and does not show area or parasitic capacitance.

Why it is a good first step: it is quick to draw and change. For y = ¬(a·b + c) the Euler path shows that the order c, a, b gives one unbroken strip on each side; trying another order on paper costs seconds, against many minutes of redrawing a full layout. It also lets the designer check the transistor count (6 crossings for this gate) against the schematic before any geometry exists.

answer.text: How design rules enter later: each line becomes a shape of rule width and each gap a rule spacing. For a two-input NAND with λ rules (contact 2λ, 1λ of diffusion round a contact, contact to gate 2λ, poly 2λ, 3λ between gates sharing an uncontacted node):

answer: The cell is about 20λ, 10 μm for λ = 0.5 μm. The stick diagram decided the order and the contacts; the rules decided the size.

Limits: at advanced nodes, layouts sit on fixed grids with restricted rules, multiple metal layers and fins, so the stick diagram is mainly a teaching and planning tool, but the Euler-path ordering it captures still drives standard-cell layout.

Using a stick diagram in practice: draw the networks, find a common Euler path, sketch the strips, poly columns, contacts and rails, then count crossings and contacts against the schematic. Only when the sketch is right are the shapes drawn to the rules, so DRC and LVS find fewer errors later.

Verdict: a stick diagram is the right first step because it fixes the decisions that are hard to change later (topology, order, sharing) and leaves the ones the rules make for you (dimensions). Check: the NAND's 4 crossings and 5 contacts in the stick match the 4 transistors and the 5 diffusion nodes that need metal in the final layout.

Light-sensitive polymer used as a temporary mask for etching or implantation.
Tool that aligns a photomask to the wafer and exposes the resist.
Dry etch using reactive ions and radicals to remove material, often anisotropically.
Film growth by chemical reaction of gases on the wafer surface.
Physical vapour deposition method that knocks target atoms onto the wafer by ion bombardment.
Thick oxide that isolates neighbouring active devices.
Thin high-quality oxide between the gate and the channel.
n-doped region built inside a p-substrate to hold PMOS transistors.
p-doped region built inside an n-substrate to hold NMOS transistors.
CMOS process that forms both an n-well and a p-well.
Growth of a crystalline silicon layer on a crystalline silicon substrate.
Low-resistance metal-silicon compound formed on poly or diffusion.
Opening that connects metal to silicon or polysilicon.
Opening that connects one metal layer to another metal layer.
Software check that a layout meets width, spacing and overlap rules.
Layout rules written as multiples of a scalable unit λ.
Topological layer sketch without dimensions, used before exact layout.
Parasitic thyristor action that can lock a CMOS circuit into a high-current state.
Heavily doped ring tied to a supply round a group of transistors; it collects injected carriers and lowers local resistance against latch-up.
Contact that ties a well or substrate to a supply and lowers parasitic resistance.
Depth at which the added dopant equals the background doping, so the type changes.
Average depth R<sub>p</sub> at which implanted ions stop; the spread around it is the straggle ΔR<sub>p</sub>.
A walk through every edge of a graph exactly once; in layout it gives the poly column order for one unbroken diffusion strip.
Source and drain implanted with the poly gate as the mask, so their edges line up with the gate without a separate alignment.
Heavily doped n<sup>+</sup> region under a BiCMOS NPN that carries collector current to the sinker with little resistance.
